outline.chapter_title: 1. Case Architecture: Procedural Background and Legal Context
outline.description: Introduces the procedural history of Jimenez v. Bondi, the parties involved, and the statutory framework governing asylum, withholding of removal, and the Convention Against Torture. This chapter sets the stage for the substantive analysis by explaining how the case ascended from an immigration judge to the Board of Immigration Appeals and finally to the Tenth Circuit under § 1252.
subtopics: Identity and status of the petitioners
Timeline of filings: NTA, IJ denial, BIA affirmation
Jurisdictional ground: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(1) and (b)(9)
Scope of the appeal and the grounds petitioners successfully contested (asylum/withholding only)
Relevant statutory definitions: refugee, protection under the Convention Against Torture

outline.chapter_title: 2. The Governing Legal Standards for Asylum
outline.description: Presents the doctrinal foundation the court applies when reviewing BIA denial of asylum rescue. It merges common law case authority with the statutory scheme, clarifying the burden of proof, the substantive elements of past persecution, nexus, well‑founded fear, and the denial of safety to the state.
subtopics: Discretionary nature of asylum under 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(1)
Burden of proof and preponderance of evidence standard
Section 1101(a)(42)(A) – definition of a refugee
Three‑step framework for past persecution (incident, protected ground, government involvement)
Well‑founded fear and government protection test
Safe relocation (fundamental change/test) and its evidentiary burden

outline.chapter_title: 3. Fact Pattern and Evaluation of the Past Persecution Claim
outline.description: Breaks down the factual controversies in the record and explains how the court weighed them under the cumulative‑effects doctrine. The analysis focuses on the differentiation between threats and actual, offensive harm, the role of partial physical harm, and the threshold for psychological impact in asylum adjudication.
subtopics: Description of threats, property dispute, and subsequent intimidation incidents
Court’s doctrine on threats versus persecution (Karki, Brandy, Chhetri, Carias‑Mejia)
Assessment of cumulative effects per Wiransane, Ritonga
Physical vs. psychological harm: when does it make the “persecution” threshold?
Petitioners’ failure to demonstrate that threats rose to persecution per precedent

outline.chapter_title: 4. Nexus Analysis: Political Opinion versus Other Motives
outline.description: Explores how the court applied the nexus requirement to assess whether Petitioners were targeted on the basis of a statutorily protected ground. It illustrates the mixed‑motive doctrine and how the evidence favored the prosecutor’s view that the primary motive was the petitioners’ involvement with the drug trafficker rather than their political activity.
subtopics: Defining a protected ground and the political opinion requirement
Mixed‑motive framework and centrality test (Rivera‑Barrientos, Dallakoti)
Evidence suggesting dominant motive: property dispute with Don Rafa
Petitioners’ lack of proof that political opinion was central
Court’s decision to reject the nexus claim

outline.chapter_title: 5. Government Protection, Safe Relocation, and Final Holding
outline.description: Shows how the court evaluated the government’s willingness and ability to protect the petitioners, the feasibility of internal relocation, and how those determinations led to denial of asylum, withholding of removal, and the refusal of review. This chapter concludes by highlighting the court’s reasoning and its implications for future cases.
subtopics: Government protection analysis: notice, response, systemic failure
Application of Aviles‑Gonzalez and Osorio‑Mora­les precedent
Evaluation of safe relocation: her stable family network and past safe residence in rural Bogotá
Implications of lacking well‑founded fear of future persecution
Court’s final decision and its reasoning hierarchy in denying the petition
